slides.title: Basic Structure of a C# Program
slides.content: A C# program consists of one or more classes. Each program needs at least one class with a Main method that serves as the entry point when the application runs.
slides.exampleOutput: Class definition; produces no console output.

slides.title: Statements and Semicolons
slides.content: Every statement in C# ends with a semicolon. This tells the compiler where one instruction ends and the next begins.

slides.title: Case Sensitivity
slides.content: C# is case-sensitive, meaning variable, method, and class names must match their declarations exactly. 'Name' and 'name' are two different identifiers.

slides.title: Comments
slides.content: Use comments to explain code. Single-line comments start with //, while multi-line comments are wrapped in /* and */.

slides.title: Blocks and Braces
slides.content: Braces {} define a block of code. Blocks group statements together and are used for class bodies, method bodies, and control structures.

slides.title: The Main Method Entry Point
slides.content: The Main method is where program execution begins. It must be static and is usually declared inside a Program class.

slides.title: Using System and Console.WriteLine
slides.content: The using System directive imports the System namespace so you can use Console.WriteLine to print output without typing the full namespace path.

slides.title: Keywords vs Identifiers
slides.content: Keywords are reserved words like class and void. Identifiers are names you choose for variables, methods, and classes. Identifiers cannot be keywords.

slides.title: Flow Builder: Statements
slides.content: Drag blocks to declare an int x, assign it 5, then output x. Each block is one statement.

exercise.prompt: Build a flow that declares x, assigns 5, and outputs x
